turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: One hundred and forty-nine? Really, Mr. Worthing, that is a most inconvenient number. It sounds dreadfully public. I must confess, I find this increasingly perplexing; a gentleman of your apparent means residing in accommodation so… temporary.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Indeed, Lady Bracknell, the number does seem… rather unremarkable, I confess. My guardian, the late Mr. Jarvis, felt it was a sensible arrangement at the time, though I’ve always understood it was merely a temporary residence, of course.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Temporary, you say? Mr. Worthing, a man of substance should not reside in a state of perpetual… transition. It suggests a certain lack of rootedness, a distressing fluidity, if you will. I trust you have given this matter considerable thought?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I assure you, I’ve given the matter of my residence considerable thought, though, as you say, it has been… somewhat dictated by circumstances. I am, in fact, currently exploring options for a more… permanent establishment, should my suit with Miss Fairfax prove successful, naturally.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: “Exploring options, Mr. Worthing? A most commendable pursuit, I must say, though rather belated in this instance. It appears you are attempting to remedy a deficiency after the fact; a most unseemly practice, wouldn't you agree?

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mamma! Must you interrogate Mr. Worthing so relentlessly? It’s quite distressing to witness, and frankly, rather unbecoming of a mother attempting to foster a… a joyful union.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Miss Fairfax, you say? A most curious addition to this already perplexing situation. I find myself compelled to inquire, Mr. Worthing, precisely what qualities you discern in Miss Fairfax that might warrant a 'suit,' as you so casually put it?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Miss Fairfax possesses a… a singular charm, Lady Bracknell, and a certain vivacity that I find most agreeable. I believe she is a most deserving young lady, and I am, naturally, hoping for her… approval. It is, of course, entirely dependent on circumstances, as I mentioned before.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Vivacity, Mr. Worthing? A rather vague and, dare I say, frivolous descriptor. I trust you are not suggesting that mere effervescence constitutes a suitable foundation for a lasting alliance? Such qualities are, naturally, fleeting; one requires substance, Mr. Worthing, substance!

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mamma! Really, substance is all very well, but surely a little vivacity isn't entirely unwelcome? Mr. Worthing clearly appreciates it, and I, for one, find it rather… refreshing.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Refreshing, you say, Gwendolen? My dear, a young lady’s sensibilities are not to be ‘refreshed’ by mere frivolity; they are to be cultivated! Mr. Worthing, I perceive a certain… lack of discernment in your choice of descriptors. Pray, elaborate on this ‘vivacity’ – I require specifics, not vague pronouncements.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Well, Lady Bracknell, when I say 'vivacity,' I mean… a sort of… spiritedness, a readiness for enjoyment, a certain… alacrity, if you will. I observe it most keenly in Miss Fairfax’s… enthusiasm for the countryside, and her… her delightful way of arranging wildflowers. It is, I assure you, quite charming.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Alacrity, Mr. Worthing? Wildflowers? I find myself struggling to connect such trivialities with the gravitas required for a suitable match. One’s appreciation for the natural world is, of course, commendable, but it scarcely constitutes a foundation upon which to build a happy home, does it? Gwendolen, do remain silent; I am addressing your suitor.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Indeed, Lady Bracknell. I quite agree that a happy home requires more than mere alacrity, though I do believe a touch of… lightness of spirit can contribute to its overall harmony. Perhaps I have not expressed myself adequately; I simply wish to convey that I find Miss Fairfax, and indeed Miss Gwendolen, to be exceptionally… agreeable companions.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Agreeable companions? Mr. Worthing, you seem determined to obfuscate the matter with platitudes! I require a man of substance, not one who merely finds young ladies 'agreeable.' Pray, tell me, do you possess any landed property?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Land? Well, Lady Bracknell, I do possess a house in the country, though it is… modest, I confess. It is quite comfortable, and I have always endeavoured to manage it responsibly, though I am, of course, not a man of great estates.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A modest house in the country? Mr. Worthing, you appear to be deliberately attempting to test my patience. One might as well propose a residence in a railway station! I trust you understand, sir, that I am not accustomed to entertaining gentlemen of such… limited resources.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I assure you, my house is quite… serviceable. While it may not rival the grand estates of some, it is well-maintained and provides a perfectly respectable environment. I am, perhaps, more accustomed to managing affairs rather than possessing vast quantities of land.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Servicable, you say? Mr. Worthing, I find your attempts at deflection most tiresome. One cannot simply 'manage affairs' and expect to be considered a suitable match for my daughter; a gentleman must *possess*, not merely *manage*!

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Lady Bracknell, I do endeavor to be resourceful, and I believe that ingenuity can sometimes compensate for a lack of inherited wealth. Surely, a man's character and principles are of greater value than the mere size of his holdings?

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Gwendolen, the carriage!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
